title: The Hill Made of a City

chapters.title: The faculty that was never finished
A tunnel and a new site
Investors, forest and a university plan

phrases.text: Climb to the top of the Teufelsberg,
a hill in the Grunewald forest in the district of Charlottenburg-Wilmersdorf,
in the western part of Berlin.
At the summit stand the domes of a Cold War listening station.
Stand there for a moment and think about what
the ground is made of. It is rubble.
The hill is the wreckage of bombed houses,
tipped here in the years after the Second World War, and since
then it has been shaped into a green area with trees.
Deep inside the hill, under all that rubble,
lies a building that was never finished.
From the top you cannot see it.
The state heritage office says it is there,
and the story of this hill starts with that building,
not with the domes.
The hill takes its name from the Teufelssee,
a lake that lies to its south in the forest.
Teufelsberg means Devil's Mountain.
Before the name was settled, German Wikipedia says,
the place was known as the rubble hill by the lake,
and the official name came only in 1972, when the tipping ended.
Its summit sits about 120 metres above sea level.
The state heritage office's newsletter calls the hill the highest artificially made
elevation in the western part of the city.
The building under it came first, though.
Its foundation stone was laid in 1937, in the years when
the Nazi state had big plans for the city.
The building was the Wehrtechnische Fakultät, a military technical faculty.
Its name means a faculty of defence technology,
and that is the first clue to its purpose.
In the office's own words it was National Socialist,
and it was never completed.
The Berlin newspaper taz ties it to Hitler's plan to
rebuild the city as the world capital Germania.
In that plan the faculty was meant to
stand in a future university town,
and the work began in the middle of the Grunewald forest.
Even the name of the man who planned it is disputed.
The state heritage office names the planner as Hans Malwitz,
a building official of the Prussian administration.
English Wikipedia credits Albert Speer with the design,
and the two sources disagree.
In 1940 the building work stopped, and it stayed unfinished through
the rest of the war and after it.
The taz says the remains still lie deep inside the hill.
Who did the building work, and how many people worked on it,
the sources consulted here do not say.
So the building sat half-built in the forest,
a shell of a college in the middle of the war,
waiting for whatever came next.
After the war, Berlin had to get rid
of the rubble of its bombed houses.
The city split in 1948, Berlin's own history pages say,
when its council was divided.
English Wikipedia says that from then on West Berlin's
debris had to stay within its own boundary.
The same article gives June 1950 as the month the West
Berlin authorities decided to open this site as a rubble dump.
From 1950 to 1972 the tipping went on,
over a period the Berliner Zeitung describes as twenty-two years.
The taz, the Berliner Zeitung and German Wikipedia
give about 26 million cubic metres in total,
while the city's sightseeing page says 25 million.
The rubble went over the college, and the hill rose above it.
Between June 1948 and May 1949 the blockade
cut West Berlin off from its supply routes.
English Wikipedia says that fuel shortages during the blockade
halted the hauling of rubble to this site,
and that once the shortages had eased,
about 600 lorries a day brought rubble to the hill.
That article cites a 1999 study by Gerhard Keiderling,
and it gives the planned volume as about 12 million cubic metres.
It also gives 14 November 1957 as the
day the ten millionth cubic metre arrived.
These figures rest on that one source, so they are attributed here,
and the picture they give is clear enough.
Who did the clearing in the city?
The Federal Agency for Civic Education, the bpb,
has an essay on the figure of the rubble woman.
In Berlin and in the Soviet zone, it says, women
were in the majority among the clearing crews in 1945 and 1946,
and women cleared rubble in every sector of the city.
In the American and French zones, by contrast,
the use of women for clearing was explicitly rejected, and in the
British zone very few women were used between 1945 and 1947.
The essay treats the rubble woman as a myth, and it concludes
that across the whole clearance women played a clearly subordinate role.
From the summer of 1945, the essay says,
city administrations in Berlin and in the towns of the Soviet zone
tried to speed up the clearing by putting the unemployed to work.
In the Nazi years, it says,
most clearing work fell to civilian workers,
prisoners of war and concentration-camp inmates.
It gives the whole of Germany about 400 million
cubic metres of rubble, though it gives no year.
The essay does not name this hill,
and no source consulted here says which crews
carried the rubble that ended up on it.
By 1972 the tipping had stopped,
and the hill was shaped into a green area.
English Wikipedia says the Senate then decided to landscape it.
The top was already in use long before that.
The state heritage office says the British had been watching the airspace
from this site since the 1950s, using mobile equipment.
In 1961 the American and British allies agreed
by contract how they would share the site.
So while the lorries were still tipping rubble on the hill,
someone had begun watching the sky from its summit,
and the rubble and the watching overlapped for more than a decade.
In April 1956, the Alliierte museum says,
Soviet army units stationed in East Germany found a tunnel that the
Americans and British had dug under East Berlin.
It ran about 450 metres,
from the American sector to the Soviet one, and its target was
the telephone lines between a Soviet military headquarters and Moscow.
Its first collection of material came on 11 May 1955, the CIA
says, and the museum gives a figure of some 440,000 calls.
The Bundesarchiv says the British built the tunnel and the Americans paid
for it, while the CIA describes a joint American and British operation.
German Wikipedia says that once the tunnel was exposed,
the American army began looking for a new site.
So why this hill, and what could anyone hear from its top?
Quick break. I'm Yusuf, and this is Walk of Berlin.
If you enjoy stories like this one,
come and walk one with me.
My walk, Berlin Then and Now,
goes from the World Clock on Alexanderplatz to Hackescher Markt,
with an archive photo at every stop.
You'll find it at walk of berlin dot com.
German Wikipedia gives a reason for the choice:
at that time the hill was the highest elevation in Berlin,
and it seemed ideal.
English Wikipedia dates the start of operations by mobile
Allied listening units on Teufelsberg to July 1961.
The taz reports that in military slang the
place was called the Field Station Berlin.
It is a plain name for a plain job:
a field station on a hill, listening to the other side.
The taz also calls the post a Horchposten, a listening post.
The sources describe those first units as mobile,
and say that permanent buildings followed from 1962 or 1963.
Nothing in the name hints at the rubble around
the summit or at the college under it.
Then came August. In the early hours of 13 August 1961,
East German security forces sealed the sector border in Berlin,
according to the Bundesarchiv, the German federal archive.
The bpb says the closure began that night with tank barriers,
barbed wire and walls,
and that the ring of troops ran around West Berlin.
Police, militia and army barricaded every access to the
western part of the city, the bpb adds.
Whole streets were cut through by provisional border installations,
which were later fortified much more heavily.
The bpb names the People's Police, the border police,
members of the workers' combat groups and the National
People's Army as the forces that sealed the ring.
Construction work that had been organised in secret beforehand then began under
the protection of those forces, the bpb says.
In the days after 13 August a wall two metres high
began to go up, according to the Bundesarchiv.
The hill stood inside the ring that had closed around West Berlin,
on the western side of the city.
English Wikipedia says its listening units had already
started work there in July.
The state heritage office says that Berlin's position in the middle
of the Eastern Bloc and the hill's height,
the highest artificial elevation in the western part of the city,
were used to listen far into the socialist states.
The state heritage office describes what the station did.
Its staff intercepted the information from telecommunications and radio traffic in West
Berlin and across the whole of the German Democratic Republic, the GDR.
The reach of the station extended into Poland and into Czechoslovakia.
According to some sources, it reached deeper, into the Soviet Union,
and the office gives that only as a claim from some sources,
not as its own finding.
The office's own title for the place is Abhörstation, listening station.
The station was part of a network of
early-warning and listening posts along the Iron Curtain,
the office says, and the phrase is the office's own.
On the summit it describes several cuboid buildings with three towers,
and radar domes covered in plastic.
In 2018 the office said that the individual buildings,
the towers and the domes still exist,
and that the site was then exposed to uncontrolled change.
The domes you can see from the
top are radar domes of the station.
German Wikipedia says new radar equipment was fitted right after 1991,
and English Wikipedia says the buildings and the radomes remain in place.
The permanent station took shape from 1962, the office says.
English Wikipedia dates the start of permanent construction to October 1963,
so the sources differ on the start.
The National Security Agency of the United States and the
British Government Communications Headquarters, GCHQ, ran the site.
German Wikipedia also names units that served there, among them the American
Army Security Agency and two Royal Air Force signal units.
The office calls the station the most
important listening post of the Western Allies.
At its peak, the office says, about 1,000 to 1,200 American staff
and about 200 to 300 British staff worked at the station.
German Wikipedia gives about 1,500 military personnel for the 1970s.
The office does not date its peak figures,
so the two cannot be checked against each other.
Those are large numbers for one hill in a forest.
The hill was a rubble dump and a listening post at the
same time, from the early 1960s until the tipping stopped in 1972.
The office gives these staff figures for the peak only,
not for the whole period.
Picture the summit in the 1960s.
On top, the towers of a listening station.
On the slopes, lorries still tipping the rubble of the city,
as they would until 1972.
Deep inside, the college that was never finished.
Three layers already lay one on top of the other.
The office places the hill in the western part of the city,
on the West Berlin side of the border,
inside the ring that had closed in August 1961.
The daily life of the people who worked up there,
their shifts, their rooms and their routines,
is not described in the sources consulted here,
so it stays out of this story.
The listening went on until East Germany fell apart,
according to English Wikipedia. The Wall came down,
and on the night of 9 November 1989 the border was opened,
the bpb says. After that, English Wikipedia says,
the station was closed and its equipment removed.
The towers and domes stayed on the summit, and the state heritage
office confirmed in 2018 that the individual buildings still exist.
The college stayed under the rubble, out of sight.
The sources show no settled use for
the hill in the years that followed.
For about thirty years, from the early 1960s to the early 1990s,
the hill had listened to the other side.
Now the other side was gone.
The towers were still standing, the domes were still on top,
and the college was still buried underneath.
The hill was a rubble hill,
a former field station and a forest all at once,
and it was not yet a monument.
Those three ways of seeing it would soon pull in different directions,
through a string of owners and plans.
So what do you do with a listening post when
the thing it was listening to has gone?
Yusuf again, one more thing before the story goes on.
If you can't join me in person,
my audio walks take you along the Berlin Wall at
Bernauer Straße and through the medieval old town,
at your own pace, on your phone.
They're at walk of berlin dot com.
The American and British forces left in 1991, the taz reports.
The state heritage office says the site was handed over in 1992,
after all its technical equipment had been removed, to Berlin's finance directorate.
The taz says the site went back to
the state of Berlin that year.
The handover came a year after the withdrawal,
so the two dates belong to two different steps.
The Berliner Zeitung describes what came next:
once the Americans and British had gone,
the decline of the grounds began.
German Wikipedia says the buildings stood empty and decayed for years afterwards,
and that for a time the site
served as a civil air-traffic radar station.
In 1996 the city sold the grounds to private investors.
The Berliner Zeitung says they paid 5.2 million marks,
and German Wikipedia gives the same sum.
English Wikipedia says the buyers planned hotels and apartments,
and that a spy museum was discussed.
German Wikipedia adds a restaurant to the list,
and dates the planning to 1998. Those plans failed.
The Berliner Zeitung calls them failed investors, and it reports that the
owners are considered to be at odds with one another.
English Wikipedia says the site has been privately owned since 1996,
and a Berlin tourism page updated in January 2026
still describes it as sold to a private investor.
The planning rules were the next obstacle.
German Wikipedia says that from April 2006 the site
was zoned as forest in Berlin's land-use plan,
and that the building permit had lapsed, because no
further building work had been carried out by the end of 2004.
English Wikipedia also gives a 2006 land-use plan that
classes the hilltop as forest. So, on paper,
the hill had become a wood where you cannot build.
The Tagesspiegel described it in exactly those terms two years later,
as forest and therefore land that could not be built on.
The sources do not say what the owners
did with the land between 2006 and 2008.
In January 2008 the Tagesspiegel reported a new plan.
The paper said that a foundation built around Maharishi,
whom it names as the founder of Transcendental Meditation,
had bought the site from the investor group,
according to its own statements,
and that it wanted to build a university on the hill.
The paper names the film director David Lynch
as a prominent supporter of the movement,
and says he had shown a model of the
planned building at the American forces' listening post.
The district's building councillor, Klaus-Dieter Gröhler,
said the district had no reason to grant a building permit.
German Wikipedia reports that in December 2008 the foundation
reportedly passed the project on to the Federal Chancellery,
which could not confirm receiving letters on the matter.
On 30 October 2018 the state heritage office
placed the whole Teufelsberg under monument protection,
as a monument area on the northern edge of the Grunewald.
The office describes three layers, one above the other.
At the bottom is the never-completed National Socialist faculty,
under the rubble hill. Above it is the postwar rubble hill.
On top is the American and British NSA Field Station,
the Cold War listening station, dated from 1962 to 1992.
The taz says the whole mountain is listed so that every
one of these historical layers is taken into account.
The reasons, the office says, are historical ones and the
hill's importance for the planning of the city.
The taz adds that the listing is not about
the place's morbid charm as a rotten place.
Senator for Culture and Europe Klaus Lederer, quoted in the office's announcement,
called the Teufelsberg a unique and many-layered monument of the twentieth century.
Many layers, in his phrase,
and the layers are exactly what the listing protects.
The office's own term is Denkmalbereich, a monument area,
and the whole hill is listed as one such area.
The reasons given are history and urban planning, not the hill's looks.
What does the listing change?
For now, nothing at all, according to the taz,
which quotes the monument office on the point.
Building work, a redesign or a demolition would first need official approval,
and the monument office would have a say in any alteration.
It is unclear, the taz writes, whether artists,
parties and film crews can keep using the site as they have.
So the listing matters mainly when someone wants to change the hill.
The paper's own verdict is that the Teufelsberg
seems to be a kind of grey zone.
What is left today is a hill in three layers,
and you can see two of them from the top.
The college lies under the rubble, out of sight.
The rubble has been shaped into a green area,
and the domes of the listening station still stand on the summit.
English Wikipedia says the landlord opened the site to visitors in the
summer of 2016, and German Wikipedia puts the
opening in the second half of the 2010s.
The site now offers public guided visits,
a 360 degree viewing platform at the top,
the Declassified exhibition and a museum called Alliierte in Berlin.
So here is the place to stand.
Go up to the viewing platform at the top and
look out over the trees and across Berlin.
Then think about the three layers under your feet.
The college at the bottom was planned for a
future university town in a capital the Nazi state wanted to build.
The rubble in the middle is the wreckage of bombed houses,
tipped here for twenty-two years.
The top is the station that listened to the other side,
and the state now protects all three layers as one monument.
The hill took twenty-two years of tipping to make,
so give it a few minutes before you go back down.
That's this week's story.
I'm Yusuf, and if you want to stand where it happened,
my walks and audio walks are at walk of berlin dot com.
phrases.display: my walks and audio walks are at walkofberlin.com.

phrases.text: Next week, another Berlin story.
